titulo.texto: Ceremonial Costume of the Flying Dancer

frase_gancho.texto: Four men descending from the sky, spinning, tied to a pole.

puente_narrativo.texto: From flights we move on to the hands that cut paper. Look for human silhouettes cut out of a brown or cream-colored paper with a rough texture.

guion_corto.texto: This is the costume worn by the Voladores (Flyers), who hurl themselves from the top of a pole more than thirty meters high. It is a striking outfit: red trousers with golden fringes, triangular scarves crossed over the chest, embroidered flowers, mirrors that reflect the sun, and a conical hat adorned with feathers and flowers. Five people take part in the ritual. Four are the Voladores, who represent the four directions of the world, and the fifth is the caporal, who plays a flute and a small drum at the top of the pole. The Voladores launch themselves tied by the feet and spin in circles until they touch the ground. It is a very ancient rite, recognized as a heritage of humanity.

guion_largo.texto:
Imagine a trunk more than thirty meters tall, without branches, planted in a plaza. At the tip, a small square frame. And on that frame, five men dressed in red, ready for something that seems impossible. This is the ritual of the Voladores, a Totonac and Nahua ceremony held in Papantla and in the highlands of Puebla, among other places, and the costume you see is the one worn for the flight.

First, the tree. It is said that, before the ritual, the community chooses a tree in the forest and asks the mountain for permission to cut it. A ceremony is held, and the trunk is carried with respect to the plaza. Perhaps that is why, for the participants, the pole is not a mere stick: it is a sacred tree that joins the earth with the sky.

Then, the characters. Four Voladores and a caporal. The caporal climbs to the top, sits on the platform, and plays a flute and a small drum while the other four launch themselves. The four Voladores are the four directions of the world, and the caporal, at the center, is the fifth: the axis. The Voladores are tied by the feet with ropes wound around the pole, and as they launch themselves they descend spinning in ever wider circles.

And now, the numbers. Each Volador makes thirteen turns before touching the ground. Four Voladores times thirteen turns makes fifty-two, which is exactly the number of years in a cycle of the Mesoamerican calendar, the one you saw on the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol). It is interpreted as a way of remembering that cycle, although not all specialists agree with this reading.

The costume is a feast of color. The red trousers, with golden fringes, recall the Sun. The crossed scarves carry mirrors and embroidered flowers, and they reflect the light as the dancers spin. The conical hat, with feathers and flowers, suggests a bird. Whoever descends with arms outstretched and wearing these adornments becomes, in a way, a bird.

The ritual is believed to be ancient, and chroniclers described it shortly after the conquest. In the reliefs and ancient figures of the Gulf Coast there are figures with bird-like features that have been linked to it. It has had to adapt over the centuries, and even so it remains alive. In two thousand nine, UNESCO inscribed it on the list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The risk is real: there is no net, and the Voladores train for years. That is why the ritual begins with prayers and offerings, and ends with relief and celebration.

Today the Voladores can be seen in Papantla, in Cuetzalan, and also in Mexico City, where they often perform on the museum’s esplanade. Some see it as a spectacle; for others, it is a prayer in the air. What is certain is that every flight is a reminder that a people can preserve a ceremony for centuries, even when the world changes around it.

texto.Region: Sierra Norte de Puebla and Totonacapan (Papantla / Cuetzalan)
texto.Technique/Material: Red velvet/satin, golden bugle-bead fringe, mirrors, feathers and embroidery
texto.Function: Sacred attire for the cosmogonic ritual of the Voladores (rain invocation)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Dance of the Flyers is a tourist spectacle invented only a few years ago.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a very ancient ritual, with roots predating the conquest. In two thousand nine UNESCO recognized it as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
